title: The One With The Memorial Service

jokes.text: Oh, great. A faster way to tell people that I'm unemployed and childless.
jokes.setup: Ross explains the alumni website lets you post messages about what you're up to.
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately frames it as a vehicle for announcing his failures.
jokes.explanation: Classic Chandler self-deprecation, perfectly in character. The quick pivot from Ross's enthusiasm to Chandler's dark spin is well-timed and character-specific. Would only work coming from Chandler.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I can't post anything on there. What am I gonna write? 'Hi, I'm Monica. I'm 40, I'm single, I'm living in my old apartment with my roommate, and I'm still waiting tables'?

jokes.text: Remember Andrea Rich? That tall girl that wouldn't sleep with you? Well, her Internet company went under, and she lost an ear in a boating accident.
jokes.setup: Ross is reading about former classmates on the alumni website.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's summary of Andrea Rich escalates from career failure to losing a body part, presented with cheerful nonchalance.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from romantic rejection to Internet bust to losing an ear is well-constructed dark comedy. The specificity of 'lost an ear in a boating accident' elevates it above a standard misfortune joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Do you remember that girl from college? What was her name... Janice?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh God, why would you bring her up? Yeah, I remember her. Why?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I ran into her yesterday. She's had quite the life.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, she got divorced twice, lost her job, her apartment flooded, she hit a parked car, and then that parked car hit another parked car.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wow. That's... that's a lot of bad luck.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not even the worst part. She sneezed on a plane and everyone got mad at her.

jokes.text: Bet she'd sleep with you now.
jokes.setup: Andrea Rich has had terrible misfortune — failed company and lost an ear.
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately ties it back to Ross's romantic rejection, suggesting her lowered circumstances make her more attainable.
jokes.explanation: Five words that land perfectly. The economy is exceptional — the entire joke is implicit. Dark but not mean-spirited in context. The best laughs often come from the shortest punchlines.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So what you're saying is... she's available?

jokes.text: No, I already e-mailed her.
jokes.setup: Chandler's dark quip implies Ross would never actually contact someone in Andrea's situation.
jokes.punchline: Ross has already done exactly that, revealing a shameless opportunism at odds with his self-presentation.
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy. Ross's self-righteous academic persona collides with his desperate romantic opportunism. The brevity and timing make it hit harder than the setup. This is Ross-specific humor at its best.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I already tried.

jokes.text: Wait a second. You split with Carol because you had different interests? I think you split with Carol because you had one very similar interest.
jokes.setup: Ross's alumni page says he split with Carol due to different interests.
jokes.punchline: Chandler points out that the real reason was they shared the same interest — in women.
jokes.explanation: Clever wordplay on 'interests' that works as both a double meaning and a character revelation. Not groundbreaking but cleanly constructed. The pivot from 'different' to 'one very similar' is well-engineered.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, at least we have that in common.

jokes.text: What, did you think you learned how to do it in the last two minutes?
jokes.setup: Ross leaves to grab his coat; Chandler and Joey are left with the computer and the alumni page.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's rhetorical question implies they're about to mess with Ross's profile, acknowledging their own bad intentions.
jokes.explanation: Functional transition joke that sets up their plotting. Decent enough but not particularly memorable. The humor lies more in the situation than the line itself.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could Ross BE any worse at this?

jokes.text: Also, I cloned a dinosaur in my lab.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey are editing Ross's alumni page to embarrass him.
jokes.punchline: The absurd addition of dinosaur cloning to Ross's profile — playing on his paleontology — escalates into absurdist territory.
jokes.explanation: Smart joke because it uses Ross's actual profession as the springboard for absurdism. It's character-specific and sets up the multi-part payoff that follows. The escalation across the three lines is well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, we should add something to Ross's alumni profile.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, like what?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't know... 'Ross Geller: Paleontologist, Professor, and part-time exotic dancer.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's good! Oh! Oh! 'Hobbies include: teaching, dinosaurs, and competitive hot dog eating.'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And 'Has never been seen in the same room as a shower curtain.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: 'Believes that leather pants are a valid fashion choice for all occasions, including court appearances.'

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: 'Distinguishing characteristics: can pronounce 'paleontology' but not 'Rachel.' Owns seventeen identical sweater vests.'

jokes.text: She is now my girlfriend.
jokes.setup: Ross allegedly cloned a dinosaur in his lab.
jokes.punchline: The cloned dinosaur is his romantic partner, escalating the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation beat. Five words that pivot from professional absurdity to romantic absurdity. Works best in sequence with the previous and following joke.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. We can explain.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, it was just a joke!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: A joke? You guys created a fake profile of me!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, we're taking it down right now.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Done. See? All gone.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Thank you. I can't believe you guys would—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, we just posted a new one.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, this time we made you look like you collect porcelain dolls and cry at night.

jokes.text: I don't care what society says, it's the best sex I've ever had.
jokes.setup: Ross is dating his cloned dinosaur.
jokes.punchline: The final beat — not only is he with the dinosaur romantically, but he's sexually involved and societally defiant about it.
jokes.explanation: The apex of a three-part escalation and the best of the trio. 'I don't care what society says' is the unexpected qualifier that makes it quotable. The specificity and defiance elevate it from merely absurd to genuinely funny. Gets a big audience laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Who hurt you?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I did.

jokes.text: It was fun. Right up until Chandler got a finger in the eye. / Who did that? / Chandler. Yeah.
jokes.setup: Rachel asks how basketball was; the natural assumption is someone else hurt Chandler.
jokes.punchline: Chandler poked himself in his own eye.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection setup — the phrasing implies external injury, the reveal is self-inflicted incompetence. Character-appropriate for Chandler and efficiently delivered across three lines.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey, don't you think you're a little too attached to Huggsy?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Too attached? I am NOT too attached to Huggsy! Huggsy is my friend, and I don't appreciate you suggesting that I'm too dependent on him. He's always there for me, he listens to me, he never judges me... Why would I be attached to that?

jokes.text: Joey, you're sure? I mean, I know how much you love him. / Rachel, let's be clear on this, okay? I do not love Huggsy. I like him a normal amount.
jokes.setup: Joey is defensive about his attachment to a stuffed penguin named Huggsy.
jokes.punchline: His denial that he 'loves' Huggsy — insisting he only likes him 'a normal amount' — is itself an admission of abnormal attachment.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'a normal amount' is the key — it's self-undermining. Joey's oblivious earnestness about his stuffed animal is perfect character comedy. The joke works because Joey genuinely believes this is a reasonable position.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? It's not mine! It's... it's a chick magnet. Chicks dig guys who have stuffed animals. It shows I'm sensitive and in touch with my feminine side.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And before you say anything, I got it as a prize at the arcade. I didn't buy it. A little kid won it for me.

jokes.text: Yeah. Well, why wouldn't she? He's a wonderful person!
jokes.setup: Rachel says Emma loves Huggsy the stuffed penguin.
jokes.punchline: Joey refers to the stuffed animal as a 'person,' revealing total lack of object/being distinction regarding Huggsy.
jokes.explanation: Joey treating the stuffed penguin as a sentient, respectable person is a great character beat. 'He's a wonderful person!' delivered with sincerity is funnier than any ironic line reading could be. Pure Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Emma is so attached to that toy. She won't go anywhere without it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, you can't blame her. That person is hilarious.

jokes.text: I've tried everything to feel better. I even tried writing a song about it... but I can't think of anything that rhymes with: [inaudible/cut off]
jokes.setup: Phoebe says she tried writing a song about the breakup but can't find a rhyme for something.
jokes.punchline: The punchline is implicit — the word she can't rhyme with Mike's name is left to audience imagination, implying something profane or absurd. The cut-off is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe — her songwriting is a recurring character trait and cutting off before the word lets the audience's imagination do the work. The structure is a well-known comedy technique but feels authentic to Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I've been trying to get over Mike by writing songs about it. I wrote one called 'My Scumbag Former Boyfriend' and I just screamed the whole thing. It was very cathartic.

jokes.text: All right, fine, I'll put another dollar in the Richard jar.
jokes.setup: Monica mentions breaking up with Richard while consoling Phoebe about Mike.
jokes.punchline: There's apparently an established penalty system (a 'Richard jar') for Monica bringing up her ex. The existence of the jar implies this happens constantly.
jokes.explanation: The 'Richard jar' is a brilliant piece of worldbuilding comedy. The implication that Monica brings up Richard so often that a financial deterrent was needed tells us everything about her character. Well-crafted because it reveals character through a system, not exposition.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You can make cruel jokes about Mike later.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I've already prepared several.

jokes.text: Oh, good, because I've already thought of three. Four! I just thought of a fourth!
jokes.setup: Phoebe says when she's ready for cruel jokes about Mike, she'll come to Monica (not now).
jokes.punchline: Monica has already pre-prepared a rotating stock of cruel jokes and updates the count in real time.
jokes.explanation: The real-time update from 'three' to 'four' is the gem here. Monica's compulsive competitive nature combined with her barely-suppressed cattiness makes this feel true to her character. The escalation mid-sentence lands as a genuine surprise.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I don't think I'm gonna see Mike anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? Why not? I thought you really liked him!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I do, but I'm just not sure about the relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh Phoebe, no! You guys are perfect together!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know what? I was just testing you.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Testing me? For what?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: To see if you'd try to talk me out of it. And you did! You really do care!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Of course I care! Why would you test me like that?

jokes.text: Unless... Am I being too crazy about this? All right, so there's no future. But that doesn't mean we still can't have fun. / You know what? Forget what I said. / Really? / All right, if that's what you want. / That was a test, and you just failed.
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells Monica to stop her from seeing Mike; then immediately second-guesses herself.
jokes.punchline: Monica almost agrees to let her off the hook, and Phoebe immediately calls it a test she failed — revealing Phoebe was testing Monica's resolve while also testing her own.
jokes.explanation: Good multi-beat gag where both characters are simultaneously failing and catching themselves. The 'that was a test' reveal is well-timed and Monica's 'Damn it! Rookie mistake!' adds the perfect button.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What did you guys write?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Just some stuff about you.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Some stuff?! It says I'm a 'paleontologist slash male nanny who collects action figures and cries during Bambi!'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, you do cry during Bambi.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's not the point! Everybody's going to read this!

jokes.text: Damn it! Rookie mistake!
jokes.setup: Monica almost let Phoebe off the hook, only to be told it was a test she failed.
jokes.punchline: Monica's self-flagellating competitive response to failing a simple emotional support task.
jokes.explanation: Monica treating a friendship support task like a competitive game she lost is pitch-perfect character comedy. 'Rookie mistake' is Monica at her most Monica — self-critical, competitive, and oblivious to social norms.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's not about dinosaur sex! It's about the paleontological implications of reproductive patterns in extinct species and how that relates to evolutionary—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Dude, you're making it worse.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, if you think about it logically, the size differential alone would create tremendous structural challenges, not to mention the biomechanical—

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, stop talking.

jokes.text: I have sex with dinosaurs?
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey posted on Ross's alumni page that he cloned a dinosaur and it's his girlfriend.
jokes.punchline: Ross reads the page and his horrified but also slightly curious-sounding question is funnier than any direct reaction.
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff to the alumni page prank. Ross's question being phrased as genuine inquiry ('I have sex with dinosaurs?') rather than outrage makes it funnier — the awkward phrasing implies he's almost processing it as new information about himself.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I beg to differ. The dinosaur sex joke is a work of comedic genius and I will not hear it slandered.

jokes.text: I believe I read that somewhere.
jokes.setup: Ross is horrified that his profile says he has sex with dinosaurs.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's mock-scholarly response as if the information is from a reputable source rather than something he fabricated.
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan. The faux-scholarly 'I believe I read that somewhere' from the person who literally wrote it is a great ironic reversal. Economy is exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't have an alumni page.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Could you BE any more defensive about that?

jokes.text: Not only is it not funny, it's physically impossible! Okay? Depending on the species, I'd have to have a 6-foot-long-- It's not funny!
jokes.setup: Ross insists the dinosaur sex joke is physically impossible.
jokes.punchline: Ross starts to explain the anatomical logistics, catching himself mid-sentence and implying he's actually thought about this.
jokes.explanation: This is the standout joke of the episode. Ross's academic instinct to fact-check and correct the record on dinosaur anatomy — even at the cost of implicating himself further — is perfect character comedy. 'Depending on the species' shows he's categorized which dinosaurs are more or less anatomically compatible with humans. The self-interruption ('I'd have to have a 6-foot-long-- It's not funny!') is a masterclass in comedic restraint. This is what Ross Geller-specific humor looks like at its finest.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey little guy. It's okay, it's okay. Uncle Joey's here. You know, I used to have a friend just like you when I was a kid. Except mine was a baseball glove, and it smelled like hot dog water. But we had some great times together. We really did.

jokes.text: I respectfully disagree.
jokes.setup: Ross says the dinosaur sex joke isn't funny.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's formal, mock-diplomatic disagreement.
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum impact in context. The formality of 'respectfully' against the content of dinosaur intercourse is the joke. Economy is perfect — but it's entirely context-dependent and not very original in isolation.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What are you doing in Emma's room?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I was just checking on her.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: At two in the morning?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She might need something.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: The only thing she needs is for you to get out!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And don't make me use this.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What is that, a scrunchie?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yes. And I will put it in your hair.

jokes.text: Oh, I respectfully disagree! [Ross reveals Chandler has his own alumni page]
jokes.setup: Chandler said 'I respectfully disagree' moments ago; Chandler claimed he has no alumni page.
jokes.punchline: Ross throws Chandler's own phrase back at him while revealing a page exists, turning the tables.
jokes.explanation: A quick and satisfying callback — Ross co-opts Chandler's own phrase to reveal the counter-attack has already begun. The mirroring is a clean, well-executed structural joke.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You take care of Huggsy, okay? And if anything happens to him...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: anything at all...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm gonna know.

jokes.text: Joey creeping into Emma's room at night to retrieve Huggsy — Rachel wakes up and threatens him with a scrunchie
jokes.setup: Joey gave Huggsy to Emma but clearly can't bear to be separated from him.
jokes.punchline: Joey is caught sneaking into a baby's room in the dark, and Rachel's 'weapon' is a hair tie.
jokes.explanation: Visual comedy inferred from dialogue — the image of Joey tiptoeing into a baby's room for a stuffed penguin while Rachel wields a scrunchie is funny. Character-perfect for Joey's childlike attachment to possessions.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross posted that you're gay?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, at least people will believe that.

jokes.text: Step away from the crib! I have a weapon! / It's okay! It's okay, Rach! It's me! Put down the scrunchie.
jokes.setup: Rachel catches an intruder in Emma's room.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'weapon' is a scrunchie — and Joey specifically names it, which grounds the absurdity in reality.
jokes.explanation: The scrunchie as weapon is the visual gag. Joey naming it specifically ('Put down the scrunchie') elevates it from implied physical comedy to explicit absurdist dialogue. Well-constructed panic comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Thank you so much! We're thrilled. Yeah, he's known for a while. Oh, there's been signs for years. Well, for one thing, he's always preferred to shop at the Gap.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And another thing — he's very organized. He color-coordinates his closet.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Plus, he's never been that into sports. He'd rather watch a musical.

jokes.text: This isn't over! [Joey whispers threateningly at the crib where Huggsy sleeps with Emma]
jokes.setup: Joey was caught trying to retrieve Huggsy from Emma's crib; he has to retreat.
jokes.punchline: Joey delivers a dramatic villain-line threat to a baby and a stuffed animal.
jokes.explanation: Joey treating a baby's crib as a heist scene requiring a dramatic exit line is excellent character comedy. The visual of this large man whispering threats at an infant and a stuffed penguin is inherently funny. Great economy — three words do all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, what? My own death?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, I had you killed off in Act Two.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You killed me?!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, you started it with the whole 'Chandler gets hit by a bus' thing.

jokes.text: Because I told everyone he slept with dinosaurs. / Well, that's clearly a joke. This could easily be true.
jokes.setup: Monica asks why Ross would post that Chandler is gay.
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately accepts the dinosaur sex claim as plausibly realistic compared to the gay claim, which inverts the obvious absurdity.
jokes.explanation: Monica's response — that dinosaur sex is 'clearly a joke' but Chandler being gay 'could easily be true' — is a sharp piece of comedy that works on multiple levels: it's a dig at Chandler, it inverts expected logic, and it's character-specific to Monica's cattiness toward her husband.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Posting my death isn't funny! How is that funny?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, it would be funny if you died in an absurdly specific way.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Like... you got killed by a bonsai tree that fell on your head while you were trying to teach it to grow in the shape of your face.

jokes.text: Yeah. Well, it came as quite a shock to me too!
jokes.setup: Monica is on the phone posing as Chandler's wife, responding to news that Chandler is gay.
jokes.punchline: Monica playing along that she's shocked by her husband's supposed homosexuality — implying she half-believes it herself.
jokes.explanation: Monica's gleeful participation in the prank at Chandler's expense while claiming to be his devastated wife is funny precisely because she enjoys it too much. The 'shock' being genuine-ish is the kicker.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Actually, did you know that more people die every year from blimp accidents than from sharks?

jokes.text: Well, I guess I should've known. He just kept making me watch Moulin Rouge.
jokes.setup: Monica is performing as shocked wife learning her husband is gay.
jokes.punchline: She ad-libs a specific 'clue' — Moulin Rouge — that she's apparently catalogued as suspicious.
jokes.explanation: The specific movie choice is funnier than a generic reference would be. Monica improvising with what seems like actual suspicion she's held onto is a nice character layer. Chandler's pained 'And that was a great movie' response makes this a two-beat joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know what? You mess with people's feelings, Chandler. It's not funny.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh come on, it's a little funny.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No it's not! I was really invested in that story about you and that girl from the copy place!

jokes.text: And that was a great movie.
jokes.setup: Monica implied Chandler's love of Moulin Rouge is evidence of his homosexuality.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's only defense is an aesthetic opinion, which does absolutely nothing to help his case.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Moulin Rouge joke. Chandler defending the movie while simultaneously digging himself deeper is exactly the kind of self-sabotage the character does. Five words that land cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, you think that's funny? You know what? I'm going to get you back. And it's going to be big. It's going to be visual. It's going to be humiliating.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm going to Xerox my butt and... and plaster them all over the building!

jokes.text: I'm dead?
jokes.setup: Chandler has posted on Ross's alumni page that he is dead.
jokes.punchline: Ross's confusion and mild existential questioning of his own mortality.
jokes.explanation: Simple reaction beat that sets up the subsequent jokes. The phrasing as a question is funnier than outrage would be. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So what are you guys doing this afternoon?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, we're gonna go home and have sex.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, in the afternoon?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Well, we don't have anything else to do.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Right, right. I mean, most people, they save that for nighttime.

jokes.text: It kills over one Americans every year.
jokes.setup: Ross protests that being killed by a blimp isn't funny.
jokes.punchline: Chandler defends the statistic with a number so small it's practically zero — 'over one' — presented as if it's a credible public health concern.
jokes.explanation: 'Over one' is an inspired piece of comedy writing. It's technically true but absurdly useless as a statistic — it means at minimum two people per year, which Chandler presents with mock gravity. This kind of precise absurdism is rare in network sitcoms. Highly quotable and stands alone out of context.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay Phoebe, calling Mike is like... it's like you're addicted to chocolate chip cookies. And every time you eat one, you tell yourself 'this is the last one,' but then twenty minutes later you're back in the kitchen with your hand in the cookie jar. And before you know it, the whole jar is empty and you're standing there with chocolate all over your face wondering how it happened. So you need to just... put the jar away. Stop calling Mike.

jokes.text: Because I'm on my way to buy some Photoshop software and a stack of gay porn. That's right. Your coming-out is about to get real graphic!
jokes.setup: Ross threatens retaliation for the death posting.
jokes.punchline: Ross's counter-threat is to Photoshop explicit gay images of Chandler and distribute them.
jokes.explanation: The prank war escalation is funny in concept but the execution is a bit broad. 'About to get real graphic' is a decent line but the setup is clunky. This works more as plot than as a crafted joke.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Here, you can use my phone.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, what is this? It's so old!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: It still works.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Does it have a rotary dial?

jokes.text: That's how it starts. 'I don't need to eat the cake, I'll just smell the icing. Why not just a little sliver? Or, okay, just a slice or two.' The next thing you know, you're 210 pounds and you get wedged in going down the tunnel slide!
jokes.setup: Phoebe says there's no harm in just calling Mike.
jokes.punchline: Monica's metaphor about resisting temptation escalates from cake-smelling to being extracted from a playground tunnel by the Jaws of Life.
jokes.explanation: Monica's food addiction is her defining trait, and using it as a metaphor for Phoebe's relationship temptation is perfect character work. The escalation from 'smelling icing' to 'Jaws of Life' is well-paced and the specificity of 210 pounds and a tunnel slide is what makes it land big. The fact that she's clearly speaking from experience makes it simultaneously funny and sad.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, it still works! It's just... retro now.

jokes.text: They had to cut me out with the Jaws of Life.
jokes.setup: Phoebe questions whether the tunnel slide story is true.
jokes.punchline: Monica confirms with matter-of-fact specificity — not just stuck, but Jaws of Life.
jokes.explanation: The confirmation that this actually happened, delivered completely straight, is the second laugh in the double-beat. Monica's calm acceptance of this humiliating memory is what makes it work — she's not embarrassed, just reporting facts.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Phoebe, can I just look in your purse for a second?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No! My purse is private!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: It's just a purse, Phoebe!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I said no! Back off, Monica!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, come on!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No way! Stop it!

jokes.text: Phoebe presents her 'current cell phone' — apparently an ancient brick phone — Monica's confused silence is the reaction
jokes.setup: Monica takes Phoebe's phones to prevent her from calling Mike.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's 'cell phone' is comically outdated — implying Phoebe operates outside of normal time and technology.
jokes.explanation: Phoebe's anachronistic cell phone is a visual gag that plays on her established character as someone out of step with modernity. Monica's incredulous 'This is your current cell phone?' is the setup and 'It reminds me of a simpler time' is the perfect Phoebe button.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, you think you're so smart, Monica Geller-Bing!

jokes.text: It reminds me of a simpler time.
jokes.setup: Monica is shocked by how outdated Phoebe's cell phone is.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's explanation frames a modern device (even if old) as nostalgic, implying she exists in a different temporal register entirely.
jokes.explanation: Five words that are entirely Phoebe. Her nostalgic relationship with an already-outdated device is consistent with her character's dreamy disconnection from reality. Clean and character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey's back! And he brought a friend.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, we can see that.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, like... a *friend* friend.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Joey brought a girl?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's what she said.

jokes.text: Damn you, Monica Geller hyphen Bing!
jokes.setup: Monica wrestles Phoebe's purse away to prevent her from calling Mike.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's frustrated curse uses Monica's full hyphenated name — the formality of the full name amplifies the comedic outrage.
jokes.explanation: The hyphenated name is the joke — using someone's full legal name in a curse is inherently funny, but 'hyphen Bing' adds an extra comedic syllable that breaks the rhythm in a satisfying way. This is the kind of line that becomes a fan favorite.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Joey! Another 'friend'? How many friends do you have?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! She's just a friend!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, right. That's what you said about the last seven 'friends.'

jokes.text: No, no, no, it's not a girl. It's... a brand-new Huggsy!
jokes.setup: Rachel is upset that Joey brought a 'girl home in the middle of the day'; Joey corrects her.
jokes.punchline: His correction isn't that he was responsible — it's that he bought an identical replacement stuffed penguin, which he presents with genuine pride.
jokes.explanation: The reveal of 'brand-new Huggsy' is funny because Joey treats it as an elegant solution when it's actually a complete failure to let go. His pride in this plan is perfect character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey! We heard you bring someone home!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, come here, I want you to meet someone really special.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Joey's finally in a serious relationship!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Everyone, I'd like you to meet... Clarence.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Clarence? That's... is that a woman's name?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no—it's a penguin. My newest addition to the collection.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, you can't keep doing this!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? He's adorable!

jokes.text: The new Huggsy. The other Huggsy, I don't know, I guess I'll just take him back.
jokes.setup: Joey proposes Emma keep the new Huggsy while he reclaims the original.
jokes.punchline: Joey plays this off as an afterthought, as if it weren't the entire point of buying the replacement.
jokes.explanation: Joey's faux-casual 'I guess I'll just take him back' is transparently self-serving and he knows it, but his delivery implies he genuinely thinks he's being generous. Good character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So when I was a little girl, I had this really special teddy bear, and every night I would...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Was it a bear, or were you just a really big baby?

jokes.text: Make the transfer!
jokes.setup: Rachel is telling a nostalgic story about her childhood pony Cotton to stall handing over Huggsy.
jokes.punchline: Joey cuts off the heartfelt story to demand immediate action on the stuffed animal swap.
jokes.explanation: Three words, perfectly timed interruption. Joey reducing Rachel's sentimental childhood memory to an inconvenience blocking his stuffed animal acquisition is hilariously selfish. The military/heist urgency of 'make the transfer' applied to a baby penguin swap is excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah, that's great, but can we talk about something important? My agent just called and I might have an audition for a big movie.

jokes.text: Should I be concerned that a button fell off the old Huggsy and I can't find it? / No, don't worry about it. I swallowed that years ago.
jokes.setup: Rachel is handling Huggsy during the transfer.
jokes.punchline: Joey casually reveals he swallowed a button off the stuffed animal years ago and has simply accepted this as a fact.
jokes.explanation: A surprise revelation joke delivered with complete nonchalance. 'I swallowed that years ago' tells us an entire story with four words — it happened long enough ago that it's just background information now, it didn't concern him then and doesn't now. Perfect Joey. The 'Hey!' after implies he catches himself and tries to pivot, making it even better.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! Huggsy's got a button eye. That's a choking hazard!

jokes.text: Oh, what? I don't think she likes the new Huggsy. / But he's the same.
jokes.setup: Joey maintains the new Huggsy is identical to the old one.
jokes.punchline: Joey's insistence that 'he's the same' while Emma clearly rejects the new penguin.
jokes.explanation: Functional running beat — Joey repeating 'but he's the same' while evidence contradicts him is a decent comedic rhythm but not particularly original. Sets up the next visual beat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I ate it.

jokes.text: You're not the same. [Joey looks in a mirror, confronting his own mortality/identity]
jokes.setup: Joey insists the new Huggsy is 'the same' as the original.
jokes.punchline: Joey catches his own reflection and delivers the line to himself — the existential realization that replacements aren't truly replacements hits him unexpectedly.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely surprising visual gag. Joey looking in a mirror and applying 'you're not the same' to himself is unexpected, philosophical, and funny. This is the best visual beat of the episode — it works both as a callback to the 'he's the same' argument and as a standalone moment of surprising Joey depth. The image of Joey having a mini-existential crisis in front of a mirror over a stuffed animal is excellent physical comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What are you talking about? They're identical!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: They're the same bear!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, they're identical!

jokes.text: You know, it's a lot less surprising to do that after I've buzzed you into the building.
jokes.setup: Monica has apparently climbed in through a window or found a surprising way into Phoebe's apartment.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's dry observation that Monica's dramatic entrance would be less alarming if she'd used the intercom.
jokes.explanation: Good deadpan line about Monica's overwrought surveillance operation. Slightly undercut by being a reaction to something we can only infer from dialogue — the visual context is missing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: They're identical! Look, same flippers, same beak, same everything!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey, they're not identical. And neither are you and Chandler, but you keep wearing the same outfit.

jokes.text: What are the chances?! One billion Chinese people, and they send Mike!
jokes.setup: Phoebe told Monica she's feeling better and ordered Chinese food; the delivery man turns out to be Mike.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's comedic calculation that one billion people could have delivered her food, but it was her ex.
jokes.explanation: Funny in its absurdist logic (Mike is not Chinese, the restaurant isn't staffed by a billion people) but the joke leans on the scenario more than the writing. Phoebe's delivery of cosmic-scale numbers is character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know, if Monica was a serial killer, she'd be really bad at it. She'd just keep surprising people until they died of heart attacks.

jokes.text: Base unit. Think, Monica, think!
jokes.setup: Phoebe called Mike using the speakerphone on the base unit of her landline while Monica had confiscated her other phones.
jokes.punchline: Monica's self-flagellating realization that she missed an obvious loophole — delivered as internal monologue/third-person self-scolding.
jokes.explanation: Monica's obsessive competitiveness turned inward is always funny. 'Think, Monica, think!' — talking to herself in the third person while scolding herself for a tactical error in what should be a friendly support role — is perfectly Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Whose shoes are these?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Those are mine.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, I thought they were Mike's. They're so... big.

jokes.text: Sorry. I guess I was thrown off by the mention of my name.
jokes.setup: Monica tells Mike 'this doesn't concern you' while he's literally being discussed.
jokes.punchline: Mike's dry acknowledgment that yes, his name being said did confuse him about whether he's involved.
jokes.explanation: Clean deadpan from Mike. The logic is impeccable — of course he was thrown off by his own name. The understatement of 'I guess I was thrown off' is a good character note for Mike as the straight man.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I ordered Chinese food.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh sure, and I'm a astronaut.

jokes.text: Make room for your friend.
jokes.setup: Monica has inserted herself between Phoebe and Mike on the couch.
jokes.punchline: She calls herself 'your friend' while performing a surveillance/restraint function that is the opposite of friendly.
jokes.explanation: The irony of Monica calling herself 'your friend' while acting as jailer/chaperone is a decent beat. Works better as a visual with her physical placement than as a standalone line.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, come on! What are the odds that the same delivery guy would mess up our order two weeks in a row? That's like a one in a million chance!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, he's delivered to us seventeen times.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, then it's a one in seventeen million chance!

jokes.text: You know, on the way over here, I saw this drunk guy throw up. And then a pigeon ate it.
jokes.setup: Phoebe and Mike are getting dangerously romantic; Monica needs to kill the mood.
jokes.punchline: Monica's conversational mood-killer is describing vomit being eaten by a pigeon — the most disgusting non-sequitur she can muster.
jokes.explanation: Monica's strategic deployment of a disgusting story to prevent romance is a great character beat. The specificity — drunk guy, vomit, pigeon eating vomit — is well-calibrated to be maximally unromantic. The scene-killing function makes it funnier than the content alone.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I have a phone in my shoe.

jokes.text: So that's what I'd look like if I worked out. And was being serviced by a policeman.
jokes.setup: Ross shows Chandler the Photoshopped gay images he made as revenge.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's response treats the images as flattering self-portraits with minor contextual quibbles.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's response subverts expectation — instead of outrage, he's mildly flattered by the physique depicted. 'Serviced by a policeman' is a funny euphemism delivered as a mundane observation. The character-specific vanity (noting the workout physique) is good.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why didn't I use speakerphone?! I could've had my hands free! I'm an idiot. A complete idiot. How do I not know about speakerphone? Everyone knows about speakerphone. I'm 30 years old and I just discovered speakerphone. What else don't I know about? Probably everything. I probably don't know how to do anything right.

jokes.text: Nobody called, nobody wrote anything, nobody cares that I'm dead!
jokes.setup: Chandler's fake Ross death announcement got no responses; Ross's coming-out got 60.
jokes.punchline: Ross's genuine distress about being ignored in his fake death — the existential wound of nobody caring.
jokes.explanation: Ross's narcissistic injury at being ignored in his fictional death is a great character beat. The specificity of comparing it to Chandler's coming-out responses makes it funnier. The lament 'nobody cares that I'm dead' as genuine grievance is very Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This conversation doesn't concern you.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: It's about me though.

jokes.text: Well, the gay community is a lot more vocal than the dead community.
jokes.setup: Ross is devastated that his fake death got zero responses while Chandler's fake coming-out got 60.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's deadpan sociological observation explains the disparity with mock-academic logic.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. The comparison is absurd — 'the dead community' doesn't exist, which is the joke — but the structure mirrors real sociological language, making it feel like genuine analysis. The underlying truth (dead people don't respond to condolences) is delivered as if it's a known fact about a constituency. Highly quotable, clean economy, works completely out of context.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm just gonna sit right here.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Monica, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Nothing! Just... sitting. On this couch. Between you two.

jokes.text: Not even my geology lab partner. And I carried that guy!
jokes.setup: Ross is upset that not one person responded to his fake death notice.
jokes.punchline: Ross reveals he did all the work in a geology lab partnership — and even this person didn't post condolences.
jokes.explanation: The idea that Ross's selfless carrying of a lab partner deserves at least a fake-death acknowledgment is a nice character beat — it reveals Ross's self-aggrandizing relationship with his academic contributions.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You're so smart and talented.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: You're so beautiful and kind.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, that's enough. You're both winners. Everybody gets a participation trophy.

jokes.text: Ross, what are you doing? / You're having a memorial service for yourself? / No, that would be stupid. You're having it for me.
jokes.setup: Ross points out there's no good outlet for grief on the website.
jokes.punchline: Ross's solution is to have Chandler host a real memorial service for Ross, while Ross is alive.
jokes.explanation: The pivot — 'No, that would be stupid. YOU're having it' — is a clean misdirection. Ross acknowledges the inherent absurdity but immediately outsources the absurdity to Chandler. Character-specific narcissism.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, that's so sweet. You guys are so cute together. Hey, that reminds me of the time I found a thumb in my garden.

jokes.text: That's all right. I'm tan, limber.... And it looks like I talked my way out of that ticket.
jokes.setup: Ross sends the Photoshopped gay images of Chandler to everyone.
jokes.punchline: Chandler finds silver linings in explicit Photoshopped images of himself — he looks tan, flexible, and apparently charming.
jokes.explanation: Chandler finding positives in explicit pictures of himself — physical appearance, apparent persuasiveness ('talked my way out of that ticket') — is a good character beat. The escalation from 'tan' to 'limber' to the ticket is well-paced.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Chandler, look at the size of that thing!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You could land a plane on that thing! I mean, what did you do, you took my face and put it on a body of a... of a really fat man!

jokes.text: Then what's that big lump under your covers? / It's Monica, okay? / That's not Monica!
jokes.setup: Rachel asks if Joey has seen Huggsy; Joey denies it.
jokes.punchline: Joey's lie that the lump under his covers is Monica is immediately seen through — but the fact that he tried 'Monica' as a cover story implies he thought this was plausible.
jokes.explanation: Joey's terrible alibi is funny — 'It's Monica, okay?' — but the comedy is in the scenario more than the writing. Rachel's immediate debunking is functional.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, nobody called? Nobody texted? Nobody posted anything on social media?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I've been gone for three days and... nothing? Not even a 'RIP Ross' meme?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm a paleontologist! I've made contributions to science! And apparently nobody cares that I'm dead!

jokes.text: Oh, don't cover its ears!
jokes.setup: Rachel is explaining to Joey why Emma loves the stuffed penguin — essentially talking about the penguin in front of it.
jokes.punchline: Joey's concern that the stuffed animal not hear something is delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Four words that reveal Joey's complete belief in Huggsy's sentience. The idea that a stuffed penguin could be hurt by overhearing a conversation is pure Joey magical thinking. Brief, perfectly timed, completely in character — one of the best single-line jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So I told them I was moving to London, and everyone freaked out. But when I said the coffee shop was closing, nobody cared.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, that makes sense. People need coffee. They don't need you.

jokes.text: No, forget it! Forget it! I can't do it! / Are you--? You're gonna take Huggsy away from a little child? / How do you think I got him in the first place?
jokes.setup: Joey almost gives Huggsy to Emma, then recants.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's moral appeal is undercut by Joey's revelation that he originally acquired Huggsy from a child — implying he has a history of this.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Joey originally stole Huggsy from a child is an excellent character-deepening joke. It recontextualizes his obsession with the toy — he's always been a child-penguin-thief — and answers the implicit question of how an adult man came to own a children's stuffed animal. Dark, surprising, and perfectly Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't believe this. I spent three hours on that lab report, and he didn't even say thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Not even a 'nice work, Ross' or a 'hey, I really appreciate you doing all the research.'

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Nothing! He just took it, looked at it for two seconds, and walked away.

jokes.text: And then it just gobbled up that puke. I mean.... That was one gross pigeon.
jokes.setup: Monica is chaperoning Phoebe and Mike; she's returned to her earlier gross-out story to kill the mood again.
jokes.punchline: Monica elaborates on the vomit-eating pigeon with what sounds like genuine aesthetic critique — the pigeon was especially disgusting.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the pigeon story, now elaborated with 'gobbled up' — an oddly specific and vivid verb choice. Monica's editorial assessment of the pigeon's grossness is funny because it implies she observed this with enough attention to form a quality judgment.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross, you can't send that invitation. It's a memorial service, not a party!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know what it is, Chandler. That's exactly why I'm sending it.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No, no, no. You're going to offend everyone. People are grieving!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Relax. I've already hit send.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: WHAT?! No!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes. And you know what? They're going to love it.

jokes.text: Oh, man. Why didn't I ask Joey to keep us apart? You throw a meatball in the hallway, we'd be doing it like rabbits right now.
jokes.setup: Phoebe reflects that Monica is a terrible choice of chaperone.
jokes.punchline: Phoebe observes that Joey — motivated by food — would have been a more effective deterrent, since distracting him is trivially easy.
jokes.explanation: A multi-character joke that works on two levels: it's a perfect Joey character comment (distracted by food instantly) and it reflects on Monica's failures as a chaperone. 'Doing it like rabbits' is a vivid image. Well-constructed and genuinely funny.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, so you're sending out invitations to your memorial service? That's great. I'm putting you down for two. You and your sense of humor.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm having my own memorial service. It's next Tuesday. I'm inviting everyone you've ever bored to death with a paleontology lecture.

jokes.text: Here's a few things you can discuss: Mucus, fungus, and the idea of me and Ross doing it.
jokes.setup: Monica announces she's going to the bathroom and needs Phoebe and Mike to discuss only unsexy topics.
jokes.punchline: Monica provides a list of approved non-romantic topics, capping it with an image of herself and Ross having sex — the most unsettling possible conversation topic.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'mucus' to 'fungus' to 'me and Ross doing it' is excellent list comedy. The third item on a list is always the punchline, and 'me and Ross doing it' is perfectly chosen — grosser than any fungus because it involves people they know, and Monica's siblings relationship makes it especially wrong.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey, what is that lump under your covers?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What lump? There's no lump.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, it's... it's my gym equipment. Yeah, I've been working out a lot.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That's your gym equipment?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: It's a very... compact routine. Look, it could also be a pillow. A really lumpy pillow that I sit on sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Joey...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Fine! It's Dwayne the Cockatoo. I found him outside and I've been keeping him as a pet.

jokes.text: Kiss him, you fool! / What? / Didn't you hear that speech? If you don't kiss him, then I will.
jokes.setup: Mike has given a heartfelt romantic speech to Phoebe; Monica was supposedly chaperoning against exactly this.
jokes.punchline: Monica, the appointed anti-romance enforcer, is so moved by the speech that she's urging Phoebe to kiss Mike — and threatening to do it herself.
jokes.explanation: The ironic reversal of Monica — the chaperone appointed to prevent this exact thing — being the one demanding the kiss is a great structural payoff. 'If you don't kiss him, then I will' is a funny threat that makes complete sense in Monica's obsessive competitive world.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: A baby's gotta have a bear. It's not unreasonable.

jokes.text: Who is this? / My friend Manny. / I asked him to keep me away from you.
jokes.setup: Monica discovers there's another man at the door after the kiss.
jokes.punchline: Mike reveals he had his own chaperone — 'Manny' — deployed for the same reason as Monica, revealing the parallel schemes.
jokes.explanation: The parallel chaperone reveal is a good structural joke — both sides were trying to prevent this meeting. The name 'Manny' is a mild added touch. Decent but doesn't maximize the comedic potential.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: She loves that penguin because it reminds her of someone.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Who?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You.

jokes.text: Hey, that's what I'm doing for Phoebe. / Well, you're not doing a very good job. / Excuse me? / What's with the kissing? / Hey, at least I knew where my guy was. / Yeah, thank God you were here to oversee all the kissing.
jokes.setup: Mike's friend Manny was supposed to keep Mike away from Phoebe; Monica was doing the same for Phoebe.
jokes.punchline: Both chaperones failed spectacularly — Manny and Monica argue about whose failure is worse while standing over the kissing couple.
jokes.explanation: The mutual chaperone failure argument is a good structural joke — two people whose only job was to prevent kissing bickering while kissing happens around them. 'Thank God you were here to oversee all the kissing' is sarcasm at its most efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey. What's with all the tears, little one? You miss your dad?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm gonna stay here with you. Yeah. Uncle Joey's not going anywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I was gonna go meet this girl... smoking hot... but you know what? She's got nothing on you.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Come here. Come here, sweetie.

jokes.text: You're heartless! / You're weak! / You're weird! / Your pants are undone.
jokes.setup: Monica and Manny are trading insults in an escalating argument.
jokes.punchline: The escalating exchange of personality insults suddenly deflates when Manny points out Monica's pants are undone — a physical detail that undercuts her moral authority.
jokes.explanation: Classic list-of-three structure extended to four, where the fourth deflates the rhythm entirely. The pivot from abstract insults ('heartless,' 'weak,' 'weird') to specific observation ('your pants are undone') is a textbook comedy structure executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, you need money? I got you, man. Here, take whatever you want.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. How much were you thinking?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, that's... that's a lot. Maybe like ten percent of that?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what, I'm gonna need that back. I'm gonna need all of that back.

jokes.text: Where'd they go? / Damn it. / Well, we blew it. / I blame myself. / And I blame you too.
jokes.setup: Monica and Manny realize Phoebe and Mike have disappeared while they were arguing.
jokes.punchline: Monica's self-blame immediately extends to also blaming Manny — a quick pivot from accountability to deflection.
jokes.explanation: 'I blame myself. And I blame you too.' is a compact comedy double-beat — the self-awareness immediately followed by finger-pointing is good Monica character comedy. The 'Well, we blew it' deadpan from Manny sets it up well.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Joey! You can't just take a toy from a baby!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why not? I took a toy from a baby once.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I was a baby.

jokes.text: I tell you, when I actually die, some people are gonna get seriously haunted.
jokes.setup: An hour has passed and no classmates have come to Ross's memorial service.
jokes.punchline: Ross's response to the social slight is to threaten post-mortem revenge via haunting — delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the episode. Ross treating haunting as a legitimate and planned future activity — 'some people are gonna get seriously haunted' — spoken with grievance and specificity is excellent. It's character-perfect (Ross's wounded pride) and genuinely surprising. The word 'seriously' does a lot of work, implying Ross has thought about the haunting regimen.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm just going to the bathroom. Don't talk about anything that would kill the romance.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't know... like dead things, or past relationships, or how you almost died that time...

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: She almost died?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Several times.

jokes.text: No, at least he died doing what he loved. / Watching blimps.
jokes.setup: Tom Gordon comes to the memorial and says he's sorry about Ross.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's eulogy frames death-by-blimp as Ross dying doing what he loved — the affectionate lie of 'watching blimps' as a passion.
jokes.explanation: Chandler's improvised eulogy is funny because 'watching blimps' is such a specific and low-stakes passion to attribute to someone. The structure ('died doing what he loved... watching blimps') is a perfect deadpan delivery of an absurd premise.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: Can't we just have one more night together?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Mike, we've been through this. You're a police officer and I'm a masseuse. It's like that song... 'A Hoedown Throwdown'... wait, no. It's like 'Romeo and Juliet' but with worse pay and better flexibility.

jokes.text: I don't remember him. But then again, I touched so many lives.
jokes.setup: Chandler tells Ross his first mourner, Tom Gordon, has arrived. Ross doesn't remember who Tom is.
jokes.punchline: Ross explains away not remembering someone who came to his memorial by implying he had too many meaningful relationships to track.
jokes.explanation: Ross's narcissistic spin on his own obscurity — 'I touched so many lives' as an excuse for not knowing someone — is a great character beat. The self-delusion is perfectly calibrated.

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I just realized we might never have another moment like this. All those times I didn't say what I was really thinking, all those moments I let slip away...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Mike, are you okay?

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, life is short and we should cherish every second we have together.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: That's sweet, but you're scaring me a little bit.

jokes.text: Actually, I barely knew him. I came because I heard Chandler's news. Do you know if he's seeing anyone?
jokes.setup: Tom Gordon came to Ross's memorial, implying deep friendship with Ross.
jokes.punchline: Tom barely knew Ross at all — he came for Chandler's coming-out news and is already trying to date him.
jokes.explanation: A good misdirection payoff — the first mourner isn't a mourner at all. The joke works on two levels: Ross's death is again irrelevant, and Chandler's fake coming-out has real consequences (romantic interest).

dialogue.speaker: Mike
dialogue.line: I came here tonight because when you realize you want to spend the rest of your life with somebody, you want the rest of your life to start as soon as possible.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, that was really romantic and I would kiss you right now, but I'm not going to because we're not supposed to see each other before the wedding and I'm not going to ruin that.

jokes.text: Yes, he is. Me. / What? You mean-- / Can I ask you a personal question? How do you shave your beard so close?
jokes.setup: Tom asks if Chandler is seeing anyone; Monica says yes, implying romance.
jokes.punchline: Tom is confused by Monica being a woman (not what he expected), and pivots to asking about her beard grooming — implying he thinks she might be a man.
jokes.explanation: The 'beard' question is the punchline — Tom thinks Monica might be a masculine woman, which is a dig at her and a callback to her standing in a masculine way (noted later). Somewhat cheap but lands well on the audience level.

jokes.text: I'm dead and no one cares? / I look like a man?
jokes.setup: Tom Gordon left without caring about Ross's death, and apparently thought Monica looked masculine.
jokes.punchline: Ross and Monica both have equal, parallel crises — Ross about his social irrelevance, Monica about her gender presentation — delivered as competing grievances.
jokes.explanation: Two perfectly parallel existential crises delivered simultaneously. The structural balance — 'I'm dead and no one cares? / I look like a man?' — is elegant comedy writing. Each is treated with identical gravity despite very different scales of problem. The rhythm of the exchange is what makes it land.

jokes.text: Please, one ridiculous problem at a time.
jokes.setup: Ross and Monica are simultaneously having competing crises.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's one-line adjudication — both problems are ridiculous, but we can only handle them serially.
jokes.explanation: Perfect straight-man economy. 'One ridiculous problem at a time' acknowledges both complaints as equally invalid without elaborating. Chandler's weary adjudication of his friends' vanity crises is excellent character work in minimal words.

jokes.text: And Monica, it's probably the way you stand!
jokes.setup: Monica is upset that Tom thought she looked like a man.
jokes.punchline: Ross — himself in the middle of a crisis — immediately has a theory about Monica's masculine appearance and delivers it as a helpful aside.
jokes.explanation: Ross delivering unsolicited gender-presentation advice while in the middle of his own existential crisis is a good character beat but slightly punches at Monica in a way that's cheap. The 'probably' is a funny qualifier — he's not certain but pretty sure.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, they left! They actually left!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: This is all your fault!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: My fault? How is this my fault?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what, it's half your fault and half my fault.

jokes.text: Hi. I'm here for Ross Geller's memorial service. / Kori? Kori Weston? / Yeah. / You look amazing. / And you are?
jokes.setup: A woman arrives for Ross's memorial service; Chandler recognizes her as a beautiful classmate.
jokes.punchline: Kori doesn't remember Chandler at all — 'And you are?' — despite his apparent enthusiasm.
jokes.explanation: Classic asymmetric recognition joke — one person is thrilled to see the other; the other has no idea who they are. Functional but not particularly fresh.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know what? If I die and nobody comes to my funeral, I'm going to be very upset.

jokes.text: Chandler. Chandler Bing. And I'm not gay. I'm not gay at all.
jokes.setup: Kori doesn't recognize Chandler; Chandler introduces himself and immediately addresses the elephant in the room.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's first instinct upon introducing himself to an attractive woman is to immediately protest his heterosexuality — confirming the gay rumors have spread.
jokes.explanation: The James Bond parody ('Chandler. Chandler Bing.') immediately undercut by the sexuality disclaimer is a solid structural joke. The doubling down ('not gay at all') implies he's protesting too much, which only makes things worse.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you came! I can't believe you actually came to the memorial.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Gordon
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I wouldn't miss it for the world.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Really? That's so sweet. I mean, you didn't even know him that well.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Gordon
dialogue.line: Actually, there's something I should tell you about why I'm really here.

jokes.text: And if heaven has a door, I'm sure he's pressing his ear up against it and listening intently.
jokes.setup: Kori is giving a sincere tribute to Ross — 'I'm sure that would mean a lot to him.'
jokes.punchline: Chandler's eulogy observation that Ross is definitely eavesdropping from heaven is both specific to Ross's nosy character and a barely-concealed hint that Ross is actually alive.
jokes.explanation: A multi-layered joke: it's a fake eulogy that's accurate about Ross's real behavior (he is literally listening from hiding), it uses heaven-door imagery to imply Ross's nosiness extends to the afterlife, and 'listening intently' is a very specific and funny verb choice. Works on both the in-universe and meta level.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Gordon
dialogue.line: I'm so sorry to hear about your father.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Thank you. Yeah, he died when he was stuck in the revolving door at Macy's.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Gordon
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's terrible!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, he wasn't a big man.

jokes.text: No, you didn't! / [Ross bursts out of hiding] I'm still alive! / Who did we bury?
jokes.setup: Kori regrets never asking Ross out, saying she 'missed her chance.'
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately reveals himself as alive; Kori's response — 'Who did we bury?' — is an absurdist non sequitur that implies she's so disoriented she thinks a burial happened.
jokes.explanation: 'Who did we bury?' is an unexpected response that implies a whole other absurd reality — Kori thinks there might have been an actual burial she attended. It's a one-line character note that lands as pure absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Gordon
dialogue.line: I'm really going to miss Ross. He was a great friend.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Gordon
dialogue.line: But Chandler... there's something about him I just can't ignore.

jokes.text: You sick freak! Who does that? I can't believe I had a crush on you.
jokes.setup: Ross explains the whole fake death/memorial situation and says her being here 'means more than a room full of people.'
jokes.punchline: Kori's romantic regret immediately inverts to disgust — 'you sick freak' — as the full context of what Ross did lands.
jokes.explanation: Good reversal — Kori went from 'I wish I'd asked him out' to 'I can't believe I had a crush on you' in the span of one revelation. The specificity of 'Who does that?' is a solid punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Gordon
dialogue.line: Are you available?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I'm kind of seeing someone right now.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Gordon
dialogue.line: Oh, who?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Me. I'm dating myself.

jokes.text: Did you hear that? Kori Weston had a crush on me!
jokes.setup: Kori has just called Ross a 'sick freak' and expressed regret for ever having a crush on him.
jokes.punchline: Ross's takeaway from the entire humiliating experience is exclusively the positive detail — Kori had a crush on him.
jokes.explanation: Ross is so starved for validation that he emerges from an explicitly humiliating public situation — faking his death, being called a sick freak — beaming because someone once had a crush on him. The selective attention is a perfect character capstone. This is the emotional punchline of the entire subplot and it's earned. High character-integration score because only Ross would process this experience this way.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Gordon
dialogue.line: So you're in a relationship with Monica?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, that's right.

dialogue.speaker: Tom Gordon
dialogue.line: And you trim your chest hair into the shape of a little heart?

jokes.text: No, Mom, I am not dead. / I know it's not something to kid about. / It was just a practical joke between Chandler and me, but it's over, okay?
jokes.setup: Ross's parents apparently called after seeing the death posting — confirming Chandler's earlier fear.
jokes.punchline: Ross has to reassure his mother he is alive via phone, which is the logical consequence of everything that happened.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of Ross's earlier concern about his parents finding out. Functional consequence comedy — the logical end of the prank chain. The deadpan delivery of 'I know it's not something to kid about' implies the mother is quite upset.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: My entire apartment smells like a wet dog!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: My closet is filled with nothing but women's clothes!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Monica and Rachel flooded it!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey thought it would be funny!

jokes.text: Actually, no. Even if I had died, you would not be left childless. / Monica?
jokes.setup: Ross is reassuring his mother about the fake death; she apparently expressed concern about being 'left childless.'
jokes.punchline: Ross corrects his mother by pointing out she still has Monica — implying the mother forgot she has another child, which is itself a devastating comment on Monica's status in the family.
jokes.explanation: A devastating joke that's funny because of what it implies: the Geller mother apparently forgot she has a daughter, or doesn't count Monica as adequate compensation for losing Ross. The single word 'Monica?' — delivered as a prompt — is the entire punchline. This is a great closing joke because it reactivates the Monica/Ross sibling dynamic with a new, sharper edge.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, maybe if Monica didn't slouch so much, Chandler would look more masculine by comparison.

tmdb_overview: Chandler's jokey entry on his and Ross's college website leads to a faux burial service for the allegedly dead and obviously unpopular Gellar. Meanwhile, Joey is unwilling to give his favorite stuffed animal, Hugsy, to Emma. And Phoebe asks Monica to help her avoid a post-breakup tryst with Mike.
insight: Memorial service premise sustains 99 jokes across 22 minutes with deadpan restraint.
